content: Early shoot borer attacks young sugarcane shoots and causes dead hearts. Remove and destroy affected shoots. Maintain proper field sanitation and avoid ratooning heavily infested crops.
Use pheromone traps for monitoring early shoot borer. Release Trichogramma parasitoids where recommended. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer and maintain balanced irrigation.
Top borer infestation causes spindle drying, bunchy top appearance and holes in leaves. Infested canes may show poor growth and reduced sugar recovery.
Destroy affected shoots and remove infested plant parts. Maintain field hygiene and avoid water stress. Pheromone traps and biological control methods may help reduce top borer infestation.
Internode borer damages sugarcane internodes and reduces cane quality. Holes with frass may appear on canes. Infested canes become weak and show reduced yield.
Remove severely affected canes and maintain clean field conditions. Avoid excessive nitrogen application and monitor crop regularly during active growth stages.
Pyrilla insects suck sap from leaves causing yellowing, drying and reduced plant vigor. Sticky honeydew and black sooty mould may develop on leaves.
Encourage natural enemies and maintain field sanitation. Remove heavily infested leaves when possible. Neem-based sprays may help during early infestation.
Whitefly infestation causes yellowing, drying and sticky honeydew on sugarcane leaves. Black fungal growth may develop due to honeydew secretion.
Maintain proper spacing and avoid dense crop growth. Remove severely infested leaves and encourage biological control agents. Neem-based products may help in early stages.
Scale insects suck sap from sugarcane leaves and stems causing yellowing, drying and weak cane growth. Severe infestation can reduce yield significantly.
Red rot disease causes drying of leaves and internal reddening of canes with white patches. Infected canes may emit alcoholic smell and dry gradually.
Use disease-free seed setts and resistant varieties where available. Remove and destroy infected clumps immediately. Avoid waterlogging and maintain good drainage.
Smut disease produces black whip-like structures from the cane top. Infected plants become thin, weak and produce narrow leaves.
Use healthy seed material and resistant varieties. Remove infected clumps immediately to prevent spread. Hot water treatment of seed setts may reduce infection.
Wilt disease causes yellowing, drying and shriveling of canes. Internal tissues may become discolored and plants gradually lose vigor.
Avoid ratooning affected fields and maintain crop rotation. Use healthy planting material and improve drainage conditions in the field.
Grassy shoot disease causes excessive tillering and thin grassy shoots. Plants become stunted and fail to produce healthy canes.
Remove and destroy infected clumps immediately. Use healthy seed canes and avoid planting material from infected fields.
Nitrogen deficiency causes pale green or yellow leaves and weak growth. Potassium deficiency may cause leaf scorching and poor cane development.
Excess water stagnation can weaken sugarcane roots and increase disease risk. Proper drainage and timely irrigation management are important.
Drought stress causes leaf rolling, drying and reduced cane growth. Regular irrigation and mulching may help conserve soil moisture.
